name: Bruges
lede: Bruges is a dark, greyed blue named in the 1910s for the Flemish city, a town whose dyers, painters and jewelers each left a mark on the history of color.

sections.title: The swatch and its name
sections.body: Our swatch comes from Maerz and Paul's *Dictionary of Color*, which dates the name Bruges to 1919 and puts it on plate 39, block J 7 [1]. The same plate holds Glacier Blue, first recorded in 1926 [1]. Why the color took the city's name is undocumented in the books we hold, so what follows is about the city and not a proven origin.

sections.title: A town of specialist dyers
sections.body:
In Bruges, Ghent, Ypres and the other Flemish towns, Pastoureau explains, dyers were strictly specialized [2]. A dyer licensed for red could not dye blue, and the reverse [2]. A manuscript made in Bruges in 1482 therefore shows an impossible scene: red and blue cloth in the same workshop [2].

Indigo reached Bruges in the thirteenth century, as it did London, Marseilles and Genoa, and woad growers tried to slow its import [3]. Brazilwood came later: dyers in Venice, Florence, Bruges and Nuremberg learned to draw bright pinks from it with alkaline mordants, and oranges with acid ones [4]. The old blue of [[indigo]] and the pinks of [[pink]] thus met in the same trading city.

sections.title: Painters and pigments
sections.body:
Flemish painters traveled to Antwerp and Bruges to buy their pigments, as German and French painters went to Cologne [5]. Vasari credited the invention of oil painting to "John of Bruges", meaning Jan van Eyck, who lived from about 1390 to 1441 [5]. Ball points out that van Eyck was not the first to use oil as a binder [5].

Giovanni Arnolfini, a merchant from Lucca who lived in Bruges, wore the scarlet fabrics and furs that his firm sold [6]. In van Eyck's double portrait of 1434, though, the bride's gown is green, which Finlay finds odd: newlyweds in fifteenth-century Bruges would more likely have shown their wealth in expensive kermes red [7]. Compare [[scarlet]].

sections.title: A relic and a diamond
sections.body: The Basilica of the Holy Blood in Bruges is one of the churches that claimed a relic of Christ's blood, and the relics seemed to multiply as churches competed [8]. Late in the fifteenth century a new way of faceting diamonds was invented in Bruges [9]. In 1477 Archduke Maximilian gave Mary of Burgundy the first recorded diamond engagement ring, which Finlay reads as a calculated gesture to impress more than a love token [9].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, 234 (1.0%) hold this swatch within six units of ΔE2000 over at least five per cent of the canvas, as photographed [10]. The best match is Bronzino's portrait [[painting:commons-Q27697982|Garzia de' Medici]], 1550, where the color covers 34% of the picture [10].

The earliest match is Duccio's *Nativity with the Prophets Isaiah and Ezekiel*, 1308 [10]. The color is about 2.8 times as common as average in 1300s paintings and 2.7 times in the 1400s, falling to 0.4 in the 1600s [10]. In 55% of these paintings it plays the shadow role, the darkest part of the palette [10]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test.

questions.q: In Flemish towns such as Bruges, what could a dyer licensed for red not do?
What did Archduke Maximilian give Mary of Burgundy in 1477, the first recorded example of its kind?

openers: A Bruges manuscript of 1482 shows red and blue cloth in one dye shop, something the city's guild rules forbade [2].
Look for this dark greyed blue in 1300s and 1400s paintings, where it is about 2.7 times as common as average [10].

issues: Maximilian ring: removed 'her father's court' (Mary's father Charles had died by 1477; source only says calculated to impress)
Other claims verified vs Pastoureau, Ball, Finlay
